summary: Docs-only: M4.8 split into M4.8a-c. No test and no production code, so nothing to mutate -- but each new row PRESCRIBES how its work is tested, and a weak prescription produces a weak test. I judged the prescriptions by asking what mutation survives the assertion each row names, checking each against what already exists in the tree (CountingBinStore, BatchingSequencerTest's idle/window tests, GoldenChainEntryTest, SimulatedClock, SmallPageStore, M4.1's measured salt-randomisation defect) and against the M4 SPEC's own acceptance criteria. THREE MAJORS, each with a concrete surviving mutation: (1) M4.8b makes request count the discriminator and explicitly deprecates 'the object appearing' -- which removes the only assertion that can constrain the zero-padded key grammar the same row calls load-bearing, so dropping the padding survives everything the row asks for and silently falsifies M4.8c's premise. (2) M4.8c's zero-LIST-at->5,000 constrains one verb: a backward walk from the chain head -- one of the three candidates the row itself lists -- issues zero LISTs and ~5,000 GETs and passes; the bound must be on TOTAL requests and constant in checkpoint count. Also, >5,000 is necessary but not sufficient, and the row's own reasoning slightly overstates it: against a strict zero-LIST assertion even 50 checkpoints kills list-and-take-last. (3) M4.8a's golden-files-plus-round-trip does not constrain field identity or encode determinism for a record made of two maps; deleting the encoder's ordering passes probabilistically, which is the exact defect M4.1's round-2 test review measured. Six minors: an off-by-one in K that survives a count sampled only at the end of the workload; the BatchingSequencer idle analogy not carrying, because that window is request-driven and a T-timer is not; no failure-path prescription for K/T configuration; no size assertion behind the ~38 KiB claim; no tier or seeding shape for the 5,000-checkpoint workload; and NFR-2 cited for a writer the requirement scopes to consumers.

findings.title: M4.8b prescribes request count 'not the object appearing', which removes the only assertion that can constrain the key grammar the same row calls load-bearing -- dropping the zero-padding survives every test the row asks for
findings.detail: The row says two things in successive clauses. First: 'ZERO-PADDED HEX IS LOad-BEARING, not cosmetic ... and M4.8c's discovery depends on it.' Then: 'ASSERTED BY REQUEST COUNT through CountingBinStore, not by the object appearing.' The second clause is right about cadence and wrong as the whole prescription, because 'the object appearing' is precisely the family of assertions that can see a key. SURVIVING MUTATION: format the key as "ctl/log/%s/%016x/ckpt/%s.ckpt".formatted(slot, epoch, Long.toHexString(seq)) -- or %x, or %016X, or a width of 8. Every PUT count is unchanged, every checkpoint object still exists, and the cadence tests (K, T, idle) are all green. Yet lexicographic order stops being numeric order at seq 0x10: "...ckpt/10.ckpt" sorts before "...ckpt/9.ckpt". Nothing in M4.8b fails, and M4.8c is then built on a premise that is false in the tree. The same hole covers the <epoch:016x> component and the .ckpt suffix. THE FIX IS ONE CLAUSE: the count assertion carries the CADENCE and a second assertion carries the GRAMMAR -- the exact key string for a seq pair whose padded and unpadded orders differ (9 and 16 is the smallest), asserted as an ORDERED pair of strings rather than merely present, plus one epoch pair. That is not 'the object appearing' (existence, which a fires-every-delta trigger also produces); it is the key as a value. Note the M4 SPEC (milestones/M4/SPEC.md:269) states the grammar as a deliverable of this milestone and no acceptance criterion in that spec asserts it either, so this row is the last place it can be caught before it is built.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8b lands green: PUT counts scale with deltas/K and seconds/T, the idle case issues nothing, and the key is written with unpadded hex. M4.8c is then implemented and tested against a store seeded by that writer, and every mechanism it can choose that relies on key order -- including the 'derive the cursor from the chain head' and 'LATEST pointer' candidates when they validate or bound a seq -- is either wrong or accidentally right on a fixture that never crosses 0x10. The failure surfaces at run time as recovery selecting checkpoint 9 over checkpoint 16 and replaying from a stale offset, and the fix is a wire-format change to a key grammar already in buckets (non-negotiable 8), not a one-line format string.

findings.title: M4.8c's zero-LIST-at->5,000 constrains one verb; a backward walk from the chain head -- a candidate this row itself lists -- issues zero LISTs and ~5,000 GETs and passes
findings.detail: The row's only prescribed assertion is 'ZERO list calls' with '>5,000 checkpoints'. SURVIVING MUTATION, and it is not hypothetical: implement discovery as the third listed candidate, 'deriving the cursor from the chain head the recovering process already holds', as a backward walk -- read the head, follow it back one object at a time until the newest checkpoint reference is found. counts().lists() is 0. counts().gets() is O(number of checkpoints). The prescribed assertion is green and the mechanism is exactly what the bound exists to forbid: the SPEC's justification (SPEC.md:279-284) is that discovery is tier 3 of M5's fallback ladder run by up to 300 plugin nodes against cost.md R15, and a path that is O(n) in a prefix growing with uptime breaches that ceiling whether the requests are LISTs or GETs. A second survivor: probe stat() upward or downward over the seq space -- zero LISTs, N STATs. THE DISCRIMINATOR THAT KILLS BOTH is a bound on TOTAL requests (counts().total(), every verb) that is CONSTANT IN THE NUMBER OF CHECKPOINTS: run discovery at two workload sizes (e.g. 500 and 5,000) and assert the totals are equal, or assert total <= a small stated constant. SECOND, AND SEPARABLE: the row's stated ground for >5,000 is subtly overstated. Against a strict zero-LIST assertion, list-and-take-last dies at 5 checkpoints, not 5,000 -- one LIST is already more than zero. What >5,000 actually buys is (a) defence against the bound being restated in PAGES, which is the round-2 defect the row cites, and (b) the second sample point that makes the constant-cost assertion above possible. Saying that is what stops the next reader treating 5,000 as sufficient, which is what the row currently reads as. The M4 SPEC's AC5 (SPEC.md:406-409) does pair 'no list at all' with 'at most K delta GETs' -- but that criterion belongs to M4.9's recovery, and M4.8c as written ships and tests discovery on its own with no GET bound at all.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8c lands with an ADR choosing chain-head derivation, a 5,000-checkpoint test asserting counts().lists() == 0, and a green suite. M4.9 then builds bounded recovery on top of it and asserts 'newest checkpoint + at most K deltas' by counting the DELTA gets it issues; the discovery walk's own GETs are either counted into a budget nobody set or attributed to the checkpoint step and waved through. Production recovery at 300 plugin nodes issues thousands of GETs per recovery on a prefix that grows with uptime -- the exact cost shape M4.8c's bound was written to forbid -- and no test in the tree fails, because the one verb anybody constrained was LIST.

findings.title: M4.8a prescribes 'encode/decode, golden files' for a record made of two maps, and neither constrains field identity nor encode determinism -- an unordered encoder passes probabilistically, which is the defect M4.1's round-2 test review measured
findings.detail: The checkpoint carries per-stream (nextOffset, oldestRetainedOffset) and per-pod lastAppliedFlushSeq -- two collections keyed by identifiers, plus two same-typed long fields sitting side by side in every stream entry. TWO MUTATIONS SURVIVE 'round-trip plus golden files' as the row states it. (a) DELETE THE ENCODER'S ORDERING (or never impose one). If the record holds a Map and encode iterates it, iteration order for Map.copyOf/HashMap is salt-randomised per JVM, so a golden file with two or three streams re-encodes to the committed bytes on most runs and not on others. This is measured history in this repo, not a worry: backlog-done.md's M4.1 row records that the missing-sort mutation was killed only PROBABILISTICALLY at three streams -- 'about 1 run in 6' -- and that raising the fixture to six streams gave 8 of 8 fresh JVMs failing. The prescription must therefore say that encode order is a stated total order and that the golden fixture carries enough entries (>=6 streams, >=2 pods) to fail in every JVM rather than most. (b) SWAP nextOffset AND oldestRetainedOffset consistently in encode and decode. Round-trip is green by construction. The golden byte-identity check catches it only if the fixture gives the two fields DISTINCT, NON-DEFAULT values -- and oldestRetainedOffset is the field the row itself says nothing consumes before M7, which is exactly the field a fixture is likely to leave at 0. The precedent that gets this right is already in the tree: GoldenChainEntryTest asserts hand-verified decoded field VALUES first and byte-identical re-encode second, and says the files were verified by hand against the layout before being committed. The row should name that shape rather than leave 'golden files' to be read as 'assert encode(decode(bytes)) == bytes', which on its own is satisfied by any self-consistent codec including a broken one.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8a lands with a three-stream golden fixture, an unsorted map encode, and oldestRetainedOffset zero everywhere. The suite is green on the author's JVM and red on roughly one CI run in six with a byte-diff nobody can reproduce locally -- the failure gets quarantined or the golden gets regenerated, which is testing.md rule 5. Meanwhile the transposed pair ships: M7's retention reads oldestRetainedOffset and gets nextOffset, deleting data that is still referenced, and the codec test that was supposed to be the tripwire for exactly this never had a value to disagree with.

findings.title: A K-trigger count sampled only at the end of the workload is insensitive to an off-by-one in K
findings.detail: 'checkpoint PUTs must scale with deltas/K' invites the test 'run N deltas with K, assert N/K PUTs'. SURVIVING MUTATION: decrement the constant, K -> K-1 (a standard constant mutant). With K=5 and 10 deltas the correct trigger fires at 5 and 10 for 2 PUTs; the mutant fires at 4 and 8, also 2 PUTs. The assertion is green. It survives whenever floor(N/K) == floor(N/(K-1)), which is most workloads a test author picks. The increment K -> K+1 happens to die at that shape, so the count assertion is half a test. FIX: prescribe that the count is sampled AT THE BOUNDARY -- zero PUTs after K-1 deltas, exactly one after the Kth, with the clock held still so T cannot supply the PUT. That kills the decrement, the increment, and 'fires on every delta' in one test.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8b ships with a trigger that checkpoints every K-1 deltas (or every K+1). Everything is green, the cost dimension the row cares about is approximately right so no dashboard notices, and M4.9's 'at most K deltas of replay' bound is quietly off by one delta in the direction that makes recovery replay more than the number stated in the spec and in the ADR.

findings.title: The BatchingSequencer idle analogy does not carry: that window is request-driven, so idleness needs no clock; a T-second timer is time-driven and 'no PUT' is only meaningful after an injected clock has moved
findings.detail: The row says the idle case 'is the same trap BatchingSequencer's window opens with its first request to avoid'. It is not the same trap. BatchingSequencer's window OPENS ON A REQUEST, so anIdleSequencerOpensNOWindowAndIssuesNOStoreRequest (BatchingSequencerTest.java:195) can prove idleness with no time passing at all, and its own comment says why: 'no wait and see nothing happened -- testing.md forbids the first and the second proves nothing a dead batcher would not also prove'. A T-second checkpoint trigger has no such structure. SURVIVING MUTATIONS if the idle test is written in that shape (construct, commit nothing, assert counts().total() == 0): (a) 'fire every T unconditionally, empty checkpoint or not' -- the clock never advanced, so it never fired, and the assertion is green while the production behaviour is the billed-idle-cluster the row exists to forbid; (b) 'the timer is never scheduled at all' -- nothing ever fires, idle is trivially green. FIX: the idle test advances an injected clock past at least 2T with zero deltas and rendezvouses on the tick having been PROCESSED before asserting (SimulatedClock is already in this module; testing.md rule 15 forbids the sleep that would otherwise close the gap), and the row's own 'idle-but-not-silent' clause -- one delta, fewer than K, clock advanced past T, exactly one PUT -- is named as the LIVENESS half that kills (b), built through the same construction path so a timer that is unscheduled in one and scheduled in the other cannot pass both.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.8b ships an idle test that constructs the writer, asserts zero requests and stops. A trigger that fires every T regardless of pending deltas passes it, and an idle 6-pod cluster writes a checkpoint per slot per T forever. That is NFR-2's failure mode, and testing.md rule 22 calls it the one failure invisible to every functional test -- which is exactly why the test that was supposed to see it must move the clock.

findings.title: K and T are 'both configuration' with no failure-path prescription (testing.md rule 14), and the tree already has the precedent for why that matters
findings.detail: SURVIVING MUTATION: accept K=0 (or negative, or T=0). K=0 means a checkpoint per delta -- a PUT rate scaling with commits, which is the cost regression this row's own sentence forbids -- and every test the row prescribes configures a sane K and T, so none of them fails. BatchingSequencer met the identical trap and the tree carries the tests for it: aZeroIntervalIsRefusedBecauseItSilentlyRestoresThePerPodRate (BatchingSequencerTest.java:309) and aNEGATIVEIntervalIsRefusedForTheSameReasonAsZero (:367). The row should ask for the analogue and say what it is defending, since 'refuse zero' looks like input validation and is actually a cost gate.
findings.failure_scenario: A Helm values file or a default constant sets checkpointEveryDeltas to 0 -- meaning 'off' to whoever wrote it -- and the writer checkpoints on every commit. No test fails, because no test ever constructs the writer with a degenerate configuration, and the bill is the first thing that notices.

findings.title: The ~38 KiB / 'deliberately not the offset->segment index' claim carries M4.8a's whole justification and has no prescribed assertion behind it
findings.detail: The row states the number twice and asserts nothing about it. Because M4.8a ships no writer, a grows-with-history test is not constructible -- but a SIZE BOUND is: encode a checkpoint at 1,600 streams (the row's own figure) and assert the encoded length is under a stated bound and is a function of stream count and pod count only, e.g. size(1,600 streams) is within a small factor of 2 * size(800 streams) and independent of the offsets' magnitude. Without it the 'no index' property is enforced by nothing but the field list of a record, and the M4 SPEC's own test table (SPEC.md:465) prescribes only 'Checkpoint round-trip; contents omit the full offset->segment index' -- a criterion with no stated assertion, which is how it comes to be checked by reading the type rather than by running anything.
findings.failure_scenario: A later commit inlines a per-stream segment list because a reader wanted it -- the change the row says would reintroduce the unbounded read M4.9 exists to remove. The only thing that fails is the golden re-encode, which the same commit regenerates as part of a legitimate-looking format bump, and no assertion anywhere states the size property that was the reason for the design.

findings.title: The >5,000-checkpoint workload has no stated tier and no stated seeding shape, and at the project's own ~38 KiB figure that is ~190 MiB of fixture
findings.detail: The M4 SPEC puts discovery at T1 on MemoryBinStore (SPEC.md:466); the row is silent, so the size requirement arrives without the tier that makes it affordable. 5,000 realistic checkpoints at ~38 KiB is ~190 MiB held in a MemoryBinStore inside a JVM whose heap cap is declared to check-test-budget.sh. Prescribe T1, and that the 5,000 are seeded as KEYS with empty or trivial bodies -- discovery reads at most the newest one, so nothing is lost -- and note SmallPageStore is already in the module if a page boundary needs forcing rather than assuming the backend's default page size.
findings.failure_scenario: The 5,000-checkpoint test is written with real encoded checkpoints, and the sequencer suite starts dying as a JVM OOM under the memory cap -- or, worse, the author reduces the workload to make it fit and lands the 50-checkpoint version this row exists to forbid, with the size requirement satisfied only in the prose.

findings.title: NFR-2 and cost.md R3 are both scoped to CONSUMERS; the row applies them to the sequencer's checkpoint writer, and 'LOad-BEARING' is a typo
findings.detail: requirements.md:30 reads 'NFR-2 | Idle cost | zero object-store requests from consumers', and cost.md rule 3 reads 'Idle consumers issue zero requests'. The property the row wants -- an idle ingester writes no checkpoint -- is right and worth testing, but neither cited authority covers a writer. There is precedent for the loose citation (BatchingSequencerTest.java:196 cites NFR-2 the same way), which is why this is minor rather than more, but a test whose stated authority does not reach it is a test that can be argued down later by someone reading the requirement rather than the intent. Either cite the cost invariant directly (request rate may never scale with time-at-idle for a component that has nothing to write) or widen NFR-2 deliberately in the requirement, not in a backlog row. Also 'ZERO-PADDED HEX IS LOad-BEARING' -- mixed case mid-word.
findings.failure_scenario: A later session weakening or deleting the idle-checkpoint test looks up NFR-2, finds it scoped to consumers, concludes the assertion was never required of the sequencer, and drops it -- and the deletion looks justified in the commit body because the requirement it names really does not cover the writer.
